events/1302_esilio/phases/0/prompt: Autumn 1301 · Sent to Rome. The embassy is waiting at the San Piero gate. Take only three things.
events/1302_esilio/phases/0/verdict:
Tried in absence
Exiled for life
If he will not appear, burn him
events/1302_esilio/phases/1/title: Rome · The pope's audience hall · Autumn 1301
events/1302_esilio/phases/1/narrative: The Blacks want the French king's brother, Charles of Valois, to come and “make peace” in Florence. The city sends three envoys to Rome to put its case to the pope — Dante is one of them.
events/1302_esilio/phases/1/instruction: Listen carefully in the hall: who is kept, and who is sent away.
events/1302_esilio/phases/1/npcs/0/dialo: Children of Florence, why so anxious? We ask only that your city obey.
The other envoys may go home and carry Our word. This poet — he stays here with Us.
events/1302_esilio/phases/1/npcs/1/dialo: (quietly) Lord Charles of Valois has already marched north with his troops, to “make peace” in Florence.
The Holy Father says: what's your hurry? Stay a few more days.
events/1302_esilio/phases/1/npcs/2/dialo: Make peace? You don't bring a single soldier to make peace.
Keeping me here in Rome… something is about to happen in the city.
events/1302_esilio/phases/2/situation:
The pope sends the other two envoys back to Florence and keeps you alone.
At the same moment, the French king's brother Charles of Valois is marching north with an army — officially, to “make peace.”
events/1302_esilio/phases/2/options/0/te: Charles really does make peace, and both parties give ground
events/1302_esilio/phases/2/options/1/te: The Blacks open the gates to him and the Whites are crushed
events/1302_esilio/phases/2/options/2/te: The Whites hold the city and Charles goes home with nothing
events/1302_esilio/phases/2/sameNote: You guessed it. So you already know what this “peace” was — now watch it land on you.
events/1302_esilio/phases/2/diffNote: It went the other way. Watch how it happened —
events/1302_esilio/phases/2/consequence:
The Blacks opened the gates for Charles. Corso Donati came back. They burned the Whites' houses and looted the Whites' shops, for six days.
Only then came the trials.
events/1302_esilio/phases/3/title: The road home · Bad news all the way
events/1302_esilio/phases/3/travelNarrat: At last the pope lets him go. On the road home, the news is worse at every stop.
events/1302_esilio/phases/3/instruction: Click each stop along the road.
events/1302_esilio/phases/3/waypoints/0/: “Charles is in the city! He didn't lose a single soldier — the gates opened by themselves.”
events/1302_esilio/phases/3/waypoints/1/: “The Blacks opened the gates for Charles, and Corso Donati is back in the city. They're burning the Whites' houses and looting the Whites' shops.”
events/1302_esilio/phases/3/waypoints/2/: “The new government is trying the Whites without them there… Signor Alighieri — you're on the list.”
events/1302_esilio/phases/4/title: Inn outside the walls · Working it out on a snowy night
events/1302_esilio/phases/4/narrative: An inn outside Florence. Snow at night. A copy of the sentence is being passed around among the White refugees. What actually happened — put the clues together.
events/1302_esilio/phases/4/instruction: Collect all 5 clues and work out what this trial really was.
events/1302_esilio/phases/4/npcs/0/dialo: “Dante Alighieri: taking bribes, extorting money he had no right to, opposing the pope and Lord Charles — a fine of five thousand florins, two years' exile, and never to hold public office again.”
Bribes? Every account I kept as prior would stand up to inspection. The charge is made up.
events/1302_esilio/phases/4/npcs/1/dialo: Confess and pay by the deadline and they cut the sentence — but confessing means admitting that the Blacks' government is the lawful one.
Confess, and you convict yourself. Refuse, and they get to take your life. Both ways are dead ends.
events/1302_esilio/phases/4/npcs/2/dialo: “The men named above have refused to appear — if any of them falls into the hands of the commune, let him be burned with fire until he dies. (igne comburatur sic quod moriatur)”
The stake. They mean to burn me alive.
events/1302_esilio/phases/4/npcs/3/dialo: Your lady asked me to bring word: “Gemma is staying in the city with the children. She is a Donati daughter — the Blacks will not touch her.”
“Don't come back.” — that was all your lady said.
events/1302_esilio/phases/4/npcs/4/dialo: Fifteen men were sentenced to burn with him on 10 March. Then look at the sentence lists, batch after batch — everyone on them is a leading White. Without exception.
events/1302_esilio/phases/5/narrative: The fire is dying down. Put all the clues together — what was this trial really?
events/1302_esilio/phases/5/options/0/te: I was unlucky. I got caught in a coup.
events/1302_esilio/phases/5/options/0/re: …No. Look again: the timing, the charges, the list. Who is behind all of it?
events/1302_esilio/phases/5/options/1/te: The pope used Charles's sword to purge the Whites — I'm an enemy removed “by law”
events/1302_esilio/phases/5/options/1/re:
Boniface held me in Rome so that Charles's sword could walk in unopposed.
The Blacks held the knife, the French cleared the road, the pope moved the pieces.
The charges were fake, the trial was real — because the trial itself was the weapon.
events/1302_esilio/phases/5/conclusion/n: The charges, the timing, the list — settle on the conclusion first. Next step: prove it.
events/1302_esilio/phases/6/claim: This trial was not justice. It was a political purge that used the law as a weapon.
events/1302_esilio/phases/6/instruction: Out of what you saw at the inn, pick the 2 things that really support this claim.
events/1302_esilio/phases/6/items/0/text: The sentence charges him with “taking bribes and extorting money he had no right to” — but Dante was a prior for two months in all.
events/1302_esilio/phases/6/items/0/why: The charge doesn't match the facts, and from first to last not one account book was ever produced. The charge was fitted on afterwards — which means convicting him was never the point.
events/1302_esilio/phases/6/items/1/text: The fifteen men sentenced to burn with him on 10 March were all leading Whites, without exception.
events/1302_esilio/phases/6/items/1/why: If they were really investigating bribery, the list of the accused would not line up exactly with one party. A list that tidy means people were picked by party, not by crime.
events/1302_esilio/phases/6/items/2/text: The second sentence raised the punishment from fine and exile to burning.
events/1302_esilio/phases/6/items/2/why: Harsh is not the same as political. A real thief who refuses to appear could have his sentence raised too. This shows they were in a hurry, but on its own it doesn't get you to “purge.”
events/1302_esilio/phases/6/items/3/text: It was snowing in Florence the days the sentence was read out.
events/1302_esilio/phases/6/items/3/why: True, but it has nothing to do with the claim. Evidence has to hold the conclusion up. Being true is not enough.
events/1302_esilio/phases/6/items/4/text: Gemma stayed in the city with the children and was never touched — she is a Donati daughter.
events/1302_esilio/phases/6/items/4/why: This one actually pulls the other way: the Blacks kept family ties, they did not kill every White they saw. True, and important — but it does not support “the trial was a weapon.” Good reasoning means recognising which facts work against you.
events/1302_esilio/phases/6/closing:
Two are enough: the charge, and the list.
The charge doesn't fit, and yet the list covers one party exactly — so what they were handling was not a court case.
events/1302_esilio/phases/7/token/detail: 1302 · Tried in absence, exiled for life, burned if he will not appear
events/1302_esilio/phases/7/afterText:
He has an ancestor, speaking in 1300, “foretell” what had already happened in 1302:

“You shall leave behind everything you love most — that is the first arrow the bow of exile shoots.
You shall taste how salty another man's bread is, and how steep another man's stairs are.”

In that same book, he also gave everyone a new place.
events/1302_esilio/phases/8/question: These people — which realm did Dante put each of them in?
events/1302_esilio/phases/8/circles/1/la: Sins that can still be washed clean
events/1302_esilio/phases/8/circles/2/la: Sins that can never be washed clean
events/1302_esilio/phases/8/souls/0/verd: Inferno XIX: in the third ditch of the eighth circle, the men who bought and sold holy office are stuffed head-down into cracks in the rock, with only the soles of their feet left outside to burn. Dante comes to the edge of one hole. Down inside it, Nicholas III mistakes him for someone else and “foretells” that the next man to fill this hole will be Boniface. — When Dante wrote this, Boniface was still alive. He put a living man into Hell, and kept the place ready for him in advance.
events/1302_esilio/phases/8/souls/0/hint: His sin has to do with “money” and “holy office.”
events/1302_esilio/phases/8/souls/1/verd: Head of the Blacks, the man who drove Dante out of the city. Dante does not sentence him with his own hand — he has Corso's own younger brother Forese say it, up in Purgatory: “The one most to blame will be dragged along by a beast, faster and faster, all the way down to the valley where the sin is never washed clean.” (Purgatorio XXIV) Two brothers: one in Purgatory, one below.
events/1302_esilio/phases/8/souls/2/verd: Purgatorio XXIII: the gluttons are so starved that they have lost their shape, and Dante almost fails to recognise his old friend. When they were young the two of them wrote poems insulting each other — really nasty ones. Yet meeting again in Purgatory, they fall into talk as if none of it had happened. — Not everyone he loved is up above, and not everyone who did wrong is down below.
events/1302_esilio/phases/8/souls/2/hint: He is Corso's brother, but he is not Corso.
events/1302_esilio/phases/8/souls/3/metL: 1283 Florence · by the Santa Trinita bridge
events/1302_esilio/phases/8/souls/3/verd: She appears in Purgatorio XXX, takes Dante over from Virgil, and leads him all the way to the final light of Paradiso XXXIII. The girl in the crimson dress at that party, when he was nine years old, ends up as the guide for the whole poem.
events/1302_esilio/phases/8/souls/3/hint: She is the one who leads the way.
events/1302_esilio/phases/9/transitionTe: Boccaccio puts down his lecture notes.
events/1302_esilio/phases/9/dufu_reactio:
The man you just put into Hell was talking to you in Rome a quarter of an hour ago.

That is how this book was made. He did not invent a Hell —
he took Florence, and Rome, and everyone he knew in his life,
and seated them all over again, level by level.
quiz/1302_esilio/quizzes/0/question: What was Dante charged with at the 1302 trial held without him?
quiz/1302_esilio/quizzes/0/options/1: Taking bribes (the charge was made up)
quiz/1302_esilio/quizzes/0/options/3: Refusing to serve as a soldier
quiz/1302_esilio/quizzes/0/explanation: The sentence of 27 January 1302 fined him and sent him into exile for “taking bribes and extorting money he had no right to” — and no evidence was ever produced. It was a political purge: Pope Boniface VIII used Charles of Valois's sword, and the Blacks carried it out.
quiz/1302_esilio/quizzes/1/question: The second sentence, on 10 March 1302, said that if Florence caught Dante he would be punished how?
quiz/1302_esilio/quizzes/1/explanation: The second sentence says it in so many words: “if he falls into the hands of the commune, let him be burned with fire until he dies” (igne comburatur sic quod moriatur). Beheading was the changed sentence, after he refused the amnesty in 1315.
quiz/1302_esilio/quizzes/2/question:
Paradiso XVII: his ancestor Cacciaguida foretells the exile.
“You shall taste how ___ another man's bread is, and how steep another man's stairs are”
quiz/1302_esilio/quizzes/2/explanation: The exile prophecy in Paradiso XVII is one of the most famous passages in the Divine Comedy — “come sa di sale lo pane altrui.” The writing turns time around: Dante, already in exile, has his ancestor “foretell” to his 1300 self everything that has already happened.
cast/people/boniface/life/0: Trained as a scholar of Church law. Worked as a diplomat for the papal court.
cast/people/boniface/life/1: Elected pope in 1294. The pope before him, Celestine V, had stepped down on his own — and at the time there were people in Rome who said Boniface had talked him into it.
cast/people/boniface/life/2: In 1300 he held the first “Jubilee” in Christian history: anyone who came to Rome as a pilgrim was forgiven their sins. People poured into the city from all over Europe. The offerings piled up on the altar of St. Peter's like little hills, and priests stood there raking them in.
cast/people/boniface/life/3: In 1302 he issued Unam Sanctam: anyone who does not obey the pope in Rome cannot be saved. It was the highest claim papal power ever made.
cast/people/boniface/life/4: In 1303, at Anagni, men of King Philip IV of France seized him and humiliated him for three days. A month after they let him go, he died in Rome.
cast/people/boniface/withDante/0: In the autumn of 1301, Florence sent three envoys to Rome to plead its case, and Dante was one of them. He sent the other two home and kept Dante behind.
cast/people/boniface/withDante/1: At the same time, he let Charles of Valois, the French king's brother, march north with troops to “mediate” in Florence. The city opened its own gates. Then came the Blacks' coup, six days of burning and looting, and then that trial.
cast/people/corso_donati/role: Leader of the Blacks, old Florentine noble
cast/people/corso_donati/life/0: Eldest son of the Donati family. Served as chief magistrate of Bologna and of Pistoia.
cast/people/corso_donati/life/1: At Campaldino in 1289 he charged with his cavalry against orders, and won — the credit went on his record, and so did the disobedience.
cast/people/corso_donati/life/2: In 1300 the priors banished him (Dante was one of the priors who signed).
cast/people/corso_donati/life/3: In November 1301 he came back into the city with Charles of Valois and tore the Whites out by the roots. For the next few years he was the man who really ran Florence.
cast/people/corso_donati/life/4: In 1308 his own Blacks accused him of treason. He rode off to escape, Catalan mercenaries caught up with him, and he died on the road outside the city.
cast/people/corso_donati/withDante/0: Dante's wife Gemma was a Donati too — they counted as distant relatives.
cast/people/corso_donati/withDante/1: During the two months Dante was a prior in 1300, his name was on the banishment list. A year later he was back, and the name on the list was Dante's.
cast/people/forese/role: Dante's boyhood friend, Corso's younger brother
cast/people/forese/life/0: Corso's younger brother, Piccarda's older brother. Three of them in one family, and not alike at all.
cast/people/forese/life/1: He never did anything big. He ate too much, loved a good time, and was always short of money.
cast/people/forese/life/2: He died in 1296, six years before Dante's exile — he never saw the great upheaval.
cast/people/forese/withDante/0: When they were young the two of them traded a whole round of insult poems, the really nasty kind: your family is poor, your wife, your coughing in the middle of the night. A set like that is called a tenzone. Both of them kept the poems. Neither destroyed them.
cast/people/forese/withDante/1: When he died, Dante was still in Florence and had not yet gone into politics.
cast/people/beatrice_young/life/0: Her father, Folco Portinari, was one of Florence's great bankers. He paid for the building of the hospital of Santa Maria Nuova.
cast/people/beatrice_young/life/1: She married Simone de' Bardi, of a banking family.
cast/people/beatrice_young/life/2: She died in June 1290, twenty-four years old.
cast/people/beatrice_young/withDante/0: In 1274, when he was nine, he saw her for the first time at a party at her house. She was wearing a crimson dress.
cast/people/beatrice_young/withDante/1: In 1283, when they were both eighteen, she greeted him at the head of the Santa Trinita bridge — Dante wrote: in that moment I seemed to see the very limit of happiness.
cast/people/beatrice_young/withDante/2: In their whole lives they said no more than a few words to each other. After she died, he made a vow at the end of the Vita Nuova: to write about her what no one had ever written about any woman.
cast/people/brunetto/role: Notary, chancellor of the commune, teacher of Florence
cast/people/brunetto/life/0: A Guelph. After the defeat at Montaperti in 1260 he spent six years in exile in France.
cast/people/brunetto/life/1: In France, in French, he wrote the big book of his life, the Trésor — an encyclopedia meant to hold all the learning in the world. His reason: French goes further, more people read it.
cast/people/brunetto/life/2: He also wrote a much shorter verse book in everyday Italian, the Tesoretto. In it the author loses his way in a wood, meets a goddess, and is led on a tour of the reasons behind all things.
cast/people/brunetto/life/3: He came back to the city in 1266 and rose to chancellor of the commune. Villani said he was the one who took the Florentines “from rough to fine” — who taught the city how to speak and how to argue politics.
cast/people/brunetto/withDante/0: We do not actually know how they met: no school record, no contract, not one letter.
cast/people/brunetto/withDante/1: We know there was such a teacher only because Dante later wrote about him.
cast/people/brunetto/withDante/2: What he taught was rhetoric and politics — how to make a whole city understand you. And one line Dante remembered all his life: a man can make himself immortal.
cast/people/piccarda/role: A nun, younger sister of Corso and Forese
cast/people/piccarda/life/0: The youngest child of the Donati family. Corso's sister, Forese's sister.
cast/people/piccarda/life/1: She entered the order of Saint Clare as a nun and took vows for life.
cast/people/piccarda/life/2: For the sake of a political marriage, her brother Corso brought men into the convent, dragged her out, and forced her to marry.
cast/people/piccarda/life/3: She fell ill and died not long after the wedding. Some say she wanted to die — her vow was broken, and she would not go on living with that.
cast/people/piccarda/withDante/0: Dante's wife Gemma was a Donati too, and the two families saw a great deal of each other.
cast/people/piccarda/withDante/1: He knew both her brothers: one was the friend he traded insults with when they were young, the other was the man who drove him out of Florence.
cast/people/cacciaguida/life/0: Born in the old Florence, when the walls were still small. People dressed plainly then, and girls marrying did not compete over dowries.
cast/people/cacciaguida/life/1: He married a woman from the Po valley whose family name was Alighieri — the name was passed down from there, and a hundred years and more later it came to Dante.
cast/people/cacciaguida/life/2: He followed the Emperor Conrad III on the Second Crusade and died fighting in the Holy Land.
cast/people/cacciaguida/withDante/0: He is Dante's great-great-grandfather, four generations back.
cast/people/cacciaguida/withDante/1: In the Paradiso, Dante claims him as his ancestor and has him tell of the old Florence — and say that line about exile: how salty another man's bread is, how steep another man's stairs are.
timeline/character/description: Author of the Divine Comedy, the first sign of the European Renaissance, “father of the Italian language”
timeline/stages/0/summary: Dante was born into a minor noble family in Florence. At nine he first saw Beatrice; as a young man he wrote the Vita Nuova. After she died, he turned to books and to a teacher.
timeline/stages/0/events/0/summary: Under the sign of Gemini, a son is born to the Alighieri. The old Florence of his ancestor Cacciaguida — and the first spark of the two parties' quarrel.
timeline/stages/0/events/1/summary: The greeting at the bridge, the battlefield of Campaldino, the death bell of 1290 — and the vow in the last chapter of the Vita Nuova.
timeline/stages/0/events/2/summary: After Beatrice died, he buried himself in books. The most learned old man in the city taught him rhetoric, politics, and one line he did not understand yet.
timeline/stages/0/events/2/comedyAnchor/: Sand under rain of fire · his teacher again
timeline/stages/1/summary: Dante joined the guild of doctors and apothecaries and stepped into politics. He became a prior — and with his own hand banished his closest friend.
timeline/stages/1/events/0/summary: Under the Ordinances of Justice, the poet joins the guild of doctors and apothecaries to win the right to take part in government. Under the surface, the Whites and the Blacks are already stirring.
timeline/stages/1/events/1/summary: Rome in its Jubilee year, Florence with Dante as prior; on the banishment list is his best friend's name. The Divine Comedy is set in this year.
timeline/stages/1/events/1/comedyAnchor/: Old Cavalcanti: where is my son?
timeline/stages/2/summary: Tried in his absence, banished for life, sentenced to burn. Under other men's roofs, Dante began to write the Divine Comedy.
timeline/stages/2/events/0/summary: The pope holds the envoy, the Blacks seize the city, the trial goes on without him: a fine, exile, and burning if he will not confess. He never set foot in Florence again.
timeline/stages/2/events/0/comedyAnchor/: Another man's bread · the pope planted upside down
timeline/stages/2/events/1/summary: The shame of eating at a great lord's table, the break with the exiled Whites; the choice to write in the everyday tongue, and the words over the gate of Hell.
timeline/stages/2/events/1/comedyAnchor/: The words over the gate of Hell
timeline/stages/2/events/2/summary: Henry VII comes south, and Dante writes open letter after open letter, staking everything. In 1313, at Buonconvento, the emperor falls suddenly ill and dies. The dream breaks.
timeline/stages/2/events/2/comedyAnchor/: The empty seat kept for Henry
timeline/stages/2/events/3/summary: Pay the fine, put on the penitent's robe, walk through the streets to the Baptistery — and he could go home. He refused: “Home by that road? Never.”
timeline/stages/2/events/3/comedyAnchor/: If ever this sacred poem brings me home
timeline/stages/3/summary: Guido Novello's welcome, his children around him again, the Paradiso finished. In September 1321 the poet was laid to rest in Ravenna.
timeline/stages/3/events/0/summary: Pine woods and golden mosaics, the test by three apostles, the fever caught on the way back from Venice, and the tale of the thirteen lost cantos.
